p: (TIMER) Thank you, Michael.

Good afternoon. My name is Witchy Carrier. I am a youth leader with the

The Committee on Education, Jointly with the 235 Committee on Public Safety Circle Keepers and a member of the Dignity in Schools Campaign. When I found out that there were more police in schools, I did not understand. There are already so many in my school. I already have to go through a metal detector. When I wear a hoodie or any kind of sweater, I already know that I will be searched. Some of you believe this will keep me safe. I do not agree. I also do not agree that immigrant services should be cut. The idea that we should have less support and more police confirms what I already know: This city sees Black and Latino boys like criminals, but I am just a child. All I want to do is go to school and hang out with my friends. Your mentality is dangerous. Also, the mentality of the gang database, which is made up of Black and Latino boys, is unacceptable. I deserve safety, care, and support, and not to be watched. This is why I support ending the use of the gang database, ending the hiring of new school police, and saying no to any bill against my rights. Thank you.

The Committee on Education, Jointly with the 236 Committee on Public Safety
You spoke and read beautifully. Thank you so much for your testimony.

HI, my name is Sika Agbokou. I am here with the Teen Activist Project, and I have a lot of experience with police presence in schools. My first extreme experience with police within my school was in middle school, and to preface, I went to the Brooklyn Science and Engineering Academy in East Flatbush. During my 8th-grade year, I was attacked and assaulted by another student twice. To note, both of these attacks were unprovoked and unwarranted, with the first happening on a staircase, and the second happening when I was on my way to go home after school, while walking downstairs from a class, which both the person and I attended. These attacks caused multiple injuries to me. The first attack caused nine lacerations to my face. However, I received zero protection from School Police Safety Members, with the other person only facing a week of in-school suspension, making me feel unsafe and unheard, after stating how I felt about the student only getting a week’s suspension.

The Committee on Education, Jointly with the 237 Committee on Public Safety The second assault caused me to visit the emergency room due to the person punching me in the head three times, biting me, and leaving me with a human bite on my left hand. After explaining the situation to a School Safety Agent, I was berated, yelled at, and reprimanded. The police in my school did not protect me and have not made me feel safe once during my entire time at school. This made me feel unsafe. Now, as a high schooler, I have witnessed many attacks, fights, and altercations between students where police merely intervened after the situation was already over. It does not feel like the police are here to keep us safe, and it does not feel like anyone is holding them accountable for it. A change is needed. To solve these issues, we need better assessments of the real issue. We need to stop school fights before they start. We need opportunities in schools to learn and practice how to manage conflicts. We need strong relationships. We need more resources. When the City Council thinks about what keeps students safe, (TIMER) please don't think about

The Committee on Education, Jointly with the 238 Committee on Public Safety easy, short-term answers. Think about creating opportunities for students to learn, grow, and build their futures. And I go to Edward R. Murrow High School in Brooklyn.
Thank you. Thank you so much to this panel for your testimony. I will now call the next panel: Cameron Glasgow Love, Kiley Bernard, and Ammy Heredia.
Sorry that I didn’t hear earlier. I was so nervous. I just want to translate everything that I said into French to represent my school and my community. (SPEAKING FRENCH)

Good afternoon. My name is Cameron. I'm 15 years old, and I live in the Cobble Hill/Boerum Hill area. I currently attend Brooklyn Collaborative Studies High School, and I'm a part of the D 39 Circle Keepers cohort and a youth leader with Dignity in Schools Campaign. I'm here today because I want the City to fully fund meaningful restorative justice programs, mental health access, and immigrant protections, and

The Committee on Education, Jointly with the 239 Committee on Public Safety divest from school police and policing infrastructure. When I first heard about them taking away the funding for these things, I was angry. The reason why is that I know from personal experience that Circle Keepers and restorative justice participants are the reason many students feel heard in school, especially during conflicts. In my experience, they have been a great help in supporting me in being able to express my feelings. Immigration protection and services are also very important. ICE has been relentless in its pursuit of immigrants, even at school, targeting Hispanics, Africans, and Caribbean immigrants, despite immigrants in the US coming from across the globe. We need to protect everybody because everyone deserves a chance to have freedom and equal chances in life. When I heard that there would be an increase in police officers, I didn't feel safe due to many cops doing their jobs completely differently based on students' ethnic backgrounds, which can

The Committee on Education, Jointly with the 240 Committee on Public Safety cause (INAUDIBLE) incidents in schools, because everyone deserves equal rights. Lastly, I love my school; we are a very diverse community, and it's a place where people from different backgrounds can come together and talk about their experiences. Less funding for Immigration Services means friends of mine will go without things that they need to thrive. I can’t imagine losing close friends because their needs were not met due to these cuts. You can keep my friends and me together by actually funding what student organizers have been fighting for because we know what’s right: Divest from school policing by rejecting Intros 175-A, 327, and 001-A (TIMER)and any legislation restricting the right to assemble or giving public dollars to private school surveillance; maintain the Mayor's veto against buffer zone bill 175-B; stop hiring any new school police; and instead expand school-based restorative justice and mental health access, including investing $80 million in hiring School Climate Coordinators in 500 schools. This is how you show students you see them as human beings, not criminals. This is how to

The Committee on Education, Jointly with the 241 Committee on Public Safety keep my school community whole. Thank you for your time.
Thank you so much for your testimony. Whenever you are ready, you may state your name for the record and begin.

Good afternoon, my name is Kiley Bernard. I'm a 10th grader at A School Without Walls and a member of the Teen Activist Project. Students are told that School Safety is there to help. However, in my many years of attending public schools, they have not shown that. I'm here to speak up for my sister. Although I have had a run-in with school safety in 7th grade, today is not only about me; it is about many kids who have been subjected, firsthand, to the safety system that is set up to fail Black and Latinx students in New York City schools. Students deserve access to resources that will improve their mental health, help them communicate their emotions, and help prevent situations that call for School Safety. Recently, my sister was attacked at her high school by a fellow student. She had all of her

The Committee on Education, Jointly with the 242 Committee on Public Safety belongings in her hand and could not fight back or defend herself. As people stood around and recorded, School Safety approached, but instead of trying to separate the two of them, she just watched. Imagine my horror when watching a video of my sister being stood over by someone who was placed there to protect her. Knowing that no one stepped in to help her, specifically School Safety, hurt even more. Fights sadly happened across New York City schools, and help should be there for all the kids who are in my sister's situation. That's not enough. Help should be there to prevent fights from happening. Unfortunately, that is not the case. Schools are in desperate need of more mental health-focused resources. Please understand that students deserve to have spaces to acknowledge, understand, and display their emotions in positive and efficient ways. Policing is not the solution, and policing will not prevent or stop fights . As explained in my previous story, kids need real help. It comes in many forms, like restorative justice programs and tight knit communities that display the importance of having

The Committee on Education, Jointly with the 243 Committee on Public Safety someone to lean on. New York City must invest in students. Thank you for your time. I hope that you take what I have said into consideration.
Thank you for your testimony. And lastly?

Hi, my name is Joelle (phonetic). I am here speaking on behalf of my friend who couldn’t make it today. “My name is Ammy. I'm a high school senior at a Community School in Brooklyn. I am also a youth leader at Make the Road New York and Urban Youth Collaborative. With the current federal administration, New York City must continue to protect immigrant students by moving away from school policing and punitive practices. I am here because I care about real safety. I do not want more police in my school or metal detectors. I want more counselors, mental health support, restorative justice, and college access. Schools should be places where students feel safe to learn and grow, and that means investing

The Committee on Education, Jointly with the 244 Committee on Public Safety in systems that truly support students instead of fueling the school to prison and deportation pipelines. In my experience, having police in my school is disruptive. Every morning, students arrive on time for school, but we are forced to stand in long lines waiting to go through scanners and metal detectors, which makes us late to class. On top of that, the school police often speak to us disrespectfully and pull students aside for extra searches. It feels like there is no way to win. Despite my best efforts to be on time and do well, I never feel welcome. Instead, I feel targeted. I have seen friends humiliated and embarrassed by unnecessary searches that turn up nothing. During a scan, they suspected my friend of hiding something under her shirt, so she was taken into the bathroom and had to lift her shirt for a full search. Nothing was found. She came out angry, and that moment stayed with her for the rest of the day. And honestly, it affected all of us who witnessed it. We all still remember that moment vividly. Experiences like this make school feel less

The Committee on Education, Jointly with the 245 Committee on Public Safety like a place of learning and more like a place where we are treated with suspicion instead of care. At the same time, I have two amazing teachers, my (INAUDIBLE) teacher and my Model UN teacher, who make me feel truly safe at school. They have supported me through difficult times and helped me grow as a student. Seeing them at school reminds me of what real support looks like. That is the kind of environment (TIMER) every student deserves, one built on care, not surveillance. We're calling on the City Council to make a different choice. Students should not be criminalized for walking into school. We should feel safe and supported, not targeted. True safety means care and community, not police or ICE. Stop filling vacant school cop positions; fund us instead. It's time to invest in counselors, mental health, and restorative justice. It's time to invest in us. Thank you for your time.”

Thank you so much for your testimony. Thank you to this panel. I appreciate it.

All right, we'll go from left to right. And I have to warn this panel to please keep it to two minutes, as opposed to the youth. I'm going to insist that you keep your remarks to two minutes, okay? All right. Thank you. You may start on my left, your right, and we'll go from there.

Good afternoon, and thank you for the opportunity to testify regarding the School Safety in New York City Public Schools. My name is Naphtali Moore. I'm a staff attorney with Advocates for Children, also known as AFC, and we're also members of the Dignity in Schools of New York. School safety requires environments that are supportive for all students and staff, yet safety is undermined when Black students and students with disabilities are treated as threats and subjected to policing rather than support. Research consistently shows that punitive responses do not improve safety and are linked to harmful long-term outcomes, while approaches like restorative justice, trauma-informed

The Committee on Education, Jointly with the 247 Committee on Public Safety care, and mental health supports improve school climate. We recently worked with a 10-year-old student with an emotional disability who was repeatedly suspended and subjected to law enforcement intervention rather than receiving appropriate supports. Police are not trained mental health professionals and should not be the primary responders to student behavior. While police interactions with children in crisis, which is when a student in emotional distress is removed from class and transported to the hospital for psychological evaluation, have declined, there are still 2,321 incidents in the 2024-2025 school year, with stark racial disparities. Black students accounted for 44% of these interventions, and 70% of the cases involved handcuffs. Too often, students with IEPs in distress are met by law enforcement instead of the trained school staff. To truly invest in school safety, the City must restore and baseline, as recommended in the City Council’s Preliminary Budget Response, two important initiatives with funding set to expire this June; sustain and baseline the $6 million in

The Committee on Education, Jointly with the 248 Committee on Public Safety Restorative Justice Funding, which helps reduce conflict and keep students in classrooms; baseline $5 million for the mental health continuum, a critical cross agency program, and invest $8 million to hire behavioral specialists, (TIMER) ensuring every district has...
Thank you.
a professional with expertise to support schools in developing effective and individualized behavior plans and reducing unnecessary suspensions and referrals to private placements.
Thank you. That last sentence was a long sentence, great.
Yes. (LAUGHS)

And I thank you for recognizing the City Council’s Preliminary Budget Response, which does seek to restore and baseline that funding for restorative justice and the mental health continuum, thank you.

Hello, my name is Imani Wilson, I'm a doctoral student candidate, actually at NYU, studying school safety, specifically here in New York City. I am also a community-based educator with

The Committee on Education, Jointly with the 249 Committee on Public Safety the Dignity in Schools Campaign, working with young people to think about transforming school safety outside of policing and punitive discipline. So in this testimony, I really want to emphasize, like a lot of the continued myths and dangerous narratives around safety that so many people in this room continue to state around the need for SSAs, metal detectors, scanning, and surveillance. Rather than addressing the root means of safety that empower and support students in New York City schools, overwhelmingly, both qualitative and quantitative education research demonstrates both the physical and psychological harm of school police presence, whether it be like carceral tools, such as metal detectors, scanners, surveillance, or even as a lot of our young people here have stated in their testimonies. So I want to just remind us that this is a big dismissal of Black and Latin@ and students with disabilities who account for over like 90% of school suspensions, arrests, and summons. And so, if we're thinking about schools being safe, do we think of them as being a priority in our implementation of school safety?

The Committee on Education, Jointly with the 250 Committee on Public Safety We invest over $400 million in policing. And even in Q-3 and Q-4 data from the NYPD, it shows that School safety Agents only resolve 12% of incidents, versus 68% are solved by DOE staff and school-based educators. And so, really thinking about where we're putting our funding, where we're investing this, and really seriously considering or reconsidering the ways that we're overwhelmingly investing in carceral punishment that has a real-life decade-long effect on our young people, who especially are Black, Latin@, Asian, and students with disabilities. I just want to urge you all to think about what we're investing in (TIMER) (CROSS-TALK)
Thank you.
And... (CROSS-TALK)
Thank you.

Good afternoon or evening. My name is Isa Abraham, and I'm the Youth Program Coordinator at Malikah, an anti-violence nonprofit in Queens and a member of the Dignity in Schools New York Coalition. I work right at the intersection of public safety and education, conducting self-defense

The Committee on Education, Jointly with the 251 Committee on Public Safety and safety trainings to community members and students who are most vulnerable to violence. The students in our programs, and their peers across New York City Public Schools, primarily students of color from working-class backgrounds, often Muslim, have been made late to class, and subject to degradation through invasive searches and surveillance by police and School Safety Agents. Only for these same schools to fail to protect them from harassment, from sometimes racist and/or Islamophobic safety school staff and administration, calling them disruptive and aggressive, even when they were the ones who were physically or verbally attacked. I recently conducted an organizing workshop with students at Metropolitan Expeditionary Learning School in the Bronx, a giant school with metal detectors and Safety Agents who were talking to me about how SSA agents and metal detectors keep them in long lines that can wrap outside the block around their school, sometimes in the rain, in the snow, and in the cold. And they cited this as a reason that contributes to why so many students just don't show up or show up halfway through the day.

The Committee on Education, Jointly with the 252 Committee on Public Safety And the weapons uncovered by these searches that the NYPD cited earlier were, by far and large, pepper spray, tasers, knives, often carried by students, if you talk to them, due to public safety issues that they encounter because they commute, right? And so these are things that community members do carry as well. So it's a much larger issue, and it requires a more holistic approach. I hope the conclusion after this hearing is that we do not need to invest in hiring more SSAs, as neither NYPD nor DOE addresses the staggering data that Council Member Gutiérrez brought up about how this policing model disproportionately affects Black and brown students. Clearly, it's a role that's not sustainable, managed well (TIMER), and no one wants to do. We need to be directing that funding towards... (CROSS-TALK)

teachers, restorative justice practitioners, and school climate.
Thank you so much.

Hello, my name is Charlotte Pope. I'm here with the New York Civil

The Committee on Education, Jointly with the 253 Committee on Public Safety Liberties Union. Thank you for the opportunity to testify. We echo the concerns of our friends from The Dignity in Schools Campaign and of the students who have long urged the City to strive for something better. We want to add to what came up earlier about metal detectors and also non-compliance with the reporting law. So for the past 10 years, through the Council's Student Safety Act, the NYPD has also been required to report on the use of metal detectors to the City Council. When we tried to FOIL that data, we learned that the NYPD was simply not giving it to you. So that's on top of the other reporting about SSAs and their placement in schools. By piecing together many other sources, we know that there are tremendous racial disparities in where metal detectors are deployed by the NYPD and that they target Bronx schools specifically. When we were part of Mayor de Blasio's leadership team on school climate, we worked to make the scanning protocols public for the first time. School communities wanted to know how to get the NYPD

The Committee on Education, Jointly with the 254 Committee on Public Safety to change its scanning designation. In that protocol, principals who believe they can transition off of scanners are ultimately pitted against a determination of the Police Commissioner, which is a huge and intimidating imbalance of power. We've confirmed with New York City Public Schools and the NYPD that principals rarely, if ever, start this process, and we know that it's not because they don't want to try. We believe this is because there's no support. None of our leaders has said it's a goal to help a school get to the point where metal detectors are no longer there. Scanners should be treated as a signal that a school is in dire need of investment and support. The Committee Report talks about how the School Construction Authority recently spent a couple of million dollars on the market's newest model of walk-through metal detector, and it is not being used the way it's marketed. We hear from school staff and students that the new equipment doesn't work to the point where students give up, they turn around and go home to avoid police harassment, and there's never any public engagement in assessing police tools.

The Committee on Education, Jointly with the 255 Committee on Public Safety Forcing students to be late to class and the long lines you mentioned are features of what scanning is. (TIMER) It's always happened from the beginning...
Thank you.

Good evening, Council Members. My name is Raul Soto. I'm the Co-Executive Director of the YA-YA Network. We're a hub of youth activism, and for the past 27 years, we have been fighting for truly safe schools, not rooted in police, but actual structures inside the school building that supports young people. The North Star remains here, very clear, that school environments need to be places where young people feel like they can learn, have programming, and form relationships with each other in a positive school climate, one that supports community building and constructive conflict resolution.

The Committee on Education, Jointly with the 256 Committee on Public Safety We just heard from a bunch of agencies kind of confirming the point that, you know, we see that, despite there not being the same number of SSAs prior to the pandemic, we're not seeing a massive explosion of incidents in these schools. It proves the case that it's not a question of a lack of SSAs, but when we're talking about restorative justice, we know that little programs in each and every school, or in some schools, not all schools, that aren't fully funded. And those are the actual structures that would keep young people safe. This isn't a question of any individual school agents. Again, some are probably wonderful people, but we're talking about how a system of predominantly students of color is treated systematically here in the city of New York. But as we heard, when we treat student safety as a question of policing, it's a model that already fails our communities. It's not something that we need to reproduce in our schools. There is concern about long lines and taking school-based roles away from their primary responsibility to conduct these activities, but instead, I ask, why are we putting so much emphasis

The Committee on Education, Jointly with the 257 Committee on Public Safety on how these schools can be doing the scanning better, rather than investing in the systems and the programs that will actually avoid these from being used in the first place? And to my colleague's point, there already is a process to evaluate how these schools can move away from scanning if the opportunity persists. If there is a question that scanning is not serving the schools by creating an operational hindrance (TIMER), we should be examining whether they're useful in those buildings.
Thank you.

Hello, I'm Andrea with Dignity in Schools, New York. Public schools should be places where young people feel safe, supported, and able to learn. Yet, there are growing calls to expand school policing and surveillance in the name of safety, despite the clear evidence that these approaches undermine student well-being and create barriers to learning, particularly for Black, brown, immigrant, transgender, and gender non-conforming students and students with disabilities. Research shows that Black students in New York City are suspended at a rate three to four times

The Committee on Education, Jointly with the 258 Committee on Public Safety that of their white peers, and are more likely to experience discipline involving the criminal justice system. Furthermore, we are facing a youth mental health crisis where nearly half of students experience symptoms of depression, and up to a quarter experience anxiety. DSC New York urges the City to reject investment in school policing and instead fund proven, effective safety strategies. Specifically, we call on the City to freeze hiring for school police, eliminate vacancies, and reinvest approximately $90 million in savings to restorative justice, mental health supports, and immigrant protections. We also urge the City to baseline $6 million in expiring restorative justice funding, while adding $2 million for additional training, and $3 million to be used for peer mediators in Circle Keepers; invest $80 million to hire school climate coordinators, in 500 priority middle and high schools; baseline $5 million for the mental health continuum, serving 50 high needs schools; protect immigrant students and families by baselining $4

The Committee on Education, Jointly with the 259 Committee on Public Safety million for outreach and communications; and passing Intro 798 to eliminate the NYP gang database. And finally, support Mayor Mamdani's veto of Intro 175-B to prevent expanded police presence around schools. Importantly, suspensions have been declining since before the pandemic and continue to decrease even amid reduced school police staffing in the mental health crisis. In 2025, suspensions dropped 8% compared to the previous year, including a 22% decline in long term suspensions. This progress reflects the increased use of restorative practices, counseling, and community-based responses that keep students engaged in school. In a study of implementation of restorative practices in Chicago high schools, researchers found 35% decline in school arrests, 50% reduction of out of school arrest (TIMER), and 18% decrease in out-of-school suspensions, and improved student-reported perceptions of school, uh... (CROSS-TALK)
Thank you.

perceptions of school climate. Thank you... (CROSS-TALK)

Good evening. My name is Tajh Sutton. The kids killed it. Dignity In Schools killed it. So I think what I want to do tonight is just root us in some history and context. This is going to be the third City Council appearance I make, while I remind this City and the Council that policing is derived from slave patrols. And as I look around at the slave owners that we have on the wall, as though they should be celebrated, I'm reminded of the often-experienced cognitive dissonance that we have in this city when we are creating policy. I want to talk about the fact that in the summer of 2020, after the murder of George Floyd, New York City Public School students made it very clear to this entire city that they wanted police removed from schools. New York City Public School students, by and large, told you tonight that they want policing-- it doesn't mean they don't want care, it doesn't mean they don't want support, it doesn't mean they don't want safety. But the data has been telling us for generations that policing does not provide that. And

The Committee on Education, Jointly with the 261 Committee on Public Safety it's not lost on me, not only who is most impacted by school policing, but who is ringing the alarm bell, and what they mean when they say safety. I'm reminded of the 660 schools from the times of segregation, and instead of calling Black and brown children wild animals and, you know, delinquent and truants, now we use the language of criminality. The Trumpian language of, you know, criminality. This man is calling our folks dog eaters, criminals, and rapists. And when we tell children that the only way they can be safe in school is to bring that entity into close proximity to them and to use that entity to police them when they want to defend their rights that we are steadily losing, particularly in the communities most impacted by policing. What are we doing? The young people who had to come after school, because we held a Public Safety and Education Hearing at 1:00 on a Wednesday, right? They were really clear. And so we need to center them (TIMER) and not any politician, think tank, organization, or funder...

Thank you.

who knows who policing will hurt the most... (CROSS-TALK)

Yeah, thank you so much, Chair Dinowitz. I would also add, respectfully, and by the way, I really appreciate all of you, your testimony, and also the really important work that you do. I hope one day we won't need any School Safety Agents, because we have no school

With continued focus and smart planning, we're confident that New York City, its boroughs, and all that it has to offer will not only host an extraordinary World Cup, but will emerge stronger and more competitive and more economically resilient because of it. I'm happy to answer questions. Thank you.

Good afternoon, Chair Maloney and members of the Economic Development Committee. My name is Ellyn Canfield and I serve alongside World Cup Czar Maya Honda as the Executive Director of New York City World Cup Operations. It's such a pleasure to be with you

today. Since our team last appeared before this committee a few months ago, we've developed an exciting platform of activities and programming designed to boost spending at local businesses, increase attendance at cultural institutions, and create opportunities for free fun and recreation for New Yorkers. Yesterday, the mayor announced that the city, in partnership with the New York-New Jersey Host Committee, will host a free official World Cup Fan Fest in each borough, reversing the prior administration's decision to charge for tickets. The Fan Fests are just one part of a much broader celebration, which will take place in plazas, parks, restaurants, commercial corridors, museums, and the myriad spaces that New Yorkers and visitors gather. My partners at NYC Tourism, as they just detailed, are developing a robust calendar which will showcase thousands of events, promotions, and activities across the boroughs. Our team was excited to see Intro 849, as it’s clear great minds think alike, particularly when it comes to a cultural passport. I'm pleased to share that we are working with Team Wonder, a collective of current and former public servants and urban planners who are developing a

physical passport connected to a digital platform. The passport, which will be published in English and Spanish, will encourage participants to visit events, exhibitions, and celebrations at participating arts and cultural institutions, libraries, parks, and community organizations across all five boroughs. Participants will collect unique stamps designed by New York City-based artists at each location, with incentives and rewards in development. The program will be free for organizations to join. In addition to World Cup-specific activations, the passport will encourage participants to explore New York City's little neighborhoods, from Little Mexico in Staten Island to Little Bangladesh in Queens. This initiative is central to the mayor's vision for the World Cup: to celebrate and showcase New York City in its— all its diversity, starting with our immigrant and diaspora communities and to encourage the flow of spending to local businesses. Our hope is that the world— is that this World Cup Cultural Passport can be a model for a longer-term passport to support the incredible institutions that make New York City a city like no other. With that, I thank you for the

opportunity to appear today and welcome any further questions.
